title: Ammar ibn Yasir
hookLine: son of Sumayyah and Yasir, forced under torture to speak against his faith, and told by the Prophet ﷺ that his heart was what mattered (16:106)

lines: THE PROPHET BRUSHES OFF THE DUST.
cards: Medina, the early days. The believers are building their mosque with their own hands, carrying mud bricks to where the walls are going up. One brick each, trip after trip.
One man is carrying two at a time. He's covered in dust. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, stops, and with his own hand brushes the dust from the man's head.
His name is Ammar. And back in Mecca, this same man broke. Today: Ammar ibn Yasir, and the heart that held.

teach.b: We met his family on an earlier day: his mother Sumayyah and his father Yasir, tortured in Mecca for their faith. Ammar was tortured too, and pushed until he said what his captors demanded, words against the Prophet.

teach.h: HOW DO YOU FIND YOUR HEART?
teach.b: A report in al-Hakim says he came to the Prophet weeping, and was asked one question: how do you find your heart? At peace with faith, he said. And he was told: if they come back to it, say it again.

Commentators connect this with a verse in Surah an-Nahl. In Pickthall's translation, it excuses the one who disbelieves under force: "save him who is forced thereto and whose heart is still content with the Faith."
Both are there: the words forced out of him, and the mercy. Now what came after.

The scene with the bricks is in Sahih al-Bukhari: everyone carried one, Ammar carried two, and the Prophet brushed the dust from him. The man who broke under torture did not spend his life as a broken man.

teach.h: PROTECTED, ON THE TONGUE OF HIS PROPHET.
teach.b: Another report in Bukhari has the companion Abu al-Darda describing Ammar as the one whom God protected from Satan on the tongue of His Prophet.
That's how the people around him remembered him: not by his worst moment, but by what was said over him afterward. Ammar's story doesn't pretend the moment didn't happen.
What it refuses is to let that moment define the whole man.
The heart held. The rest of him got up, and carried bricks.

how: Muslim jurists cite Ammar's story and Qur'an 16:106 for the ruling that someone forced under threat to speak against their faith, while the heart stays with it, is not held guilty, and Muslims remember Ammar with honor among the early believers.

o: a companion who gave up his faith under torture
a companion forced to speak, whose heart held
the builder who designed the mosque in Medina

games.q: Ammar ibn Yasir — tap the pairs.
p: how do you find your heart?

s: after he was forced to speak, Ammar was condemned
he was asked about his heart, and the verse excuses the one forced while the heart holds.
Ammar carried two bricks when others carried one
in Bukhari, and the Prophet brushed the dust from him.
the companions remembered him by his worst moment
Abu al-Darda called him the one God protected on the tongue of His Prophet.

games.q: you're Ammar. under torture you've said what they demanded, against the Prophet. you come to him weeping. what does he ask you?
o: how do you find your heart?
games.why: he asked about his heart. 'at peace with faith,' Ammar said, and he was not condemned.

practice: This week went from Hasan and Husayn and the people of the house to Bilal, Salman, Abu Dharr and Ammar.
Let one moment come back when you gave in or didn't hold, don't argue with it, and ask the question he was asked: how do you find your heart?
If you pray, ask God's forgiveness and mercy; if not, set the moment down beside you, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Ammar, forced under torture to speak against his faith, told his heart was what mattered, and remembered carrying double the bricks for the mosque. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: Ammar, son of Yasir; his mother was Sumayyah.

carryVoice: Your line: the heart held. One weak moment is not the whole person. Eight hundred twenty-six days, and counting.
